text: Hi, how's it going? I'm a big coffee lover, so I guess I'll start there. I can't really start my day without a cup of coffee, and this morning was no different. I had one before I came to take this test, and I'm already looking forward to another one once it's over. I work in IT, and my days are pretty busy. I live in an apartment, and I'm pretty much a homebody. In my free time, I like listening to music, playing computer games, and reading. So, yeah, that's me in a nutshell: coffee, music, and my computer. I'm happy to be here, and I hope I do well today!

One place I'd love to go back to is Bangkok, in Thailand. We went with some friends a few years ago. To be honest, I didn't expect much, but the city blew me away. It was loud, hot, and crowded, but it was full of energy. There were golden temples next to tall skyscrapers, and tuk-tuks zipping around everywhere. And the street food! I ate so much pad thai that I lost count. But what really got me was the people. They call Thailand "the land of smiles", and it's true. Everyone was so kind and relaxed, even when I made a mistake. When I tried to say "thank you" in Thai, the vendor smiled so big, I felt like a local. It was a feel-good trip from start to finish.

When I travel abroad, I'm not really a "tour bus" kind of guy. I'd rather wander around and see what I find. First, I always hunt for local food. I'll go to a market and point at whatever looks good! Second, I check out the local coffee shops. I'm a coffee lover, after all. I like seeing how people in other countries drink their coffee. In Vietnam, for example, they put sweet milk in it, and it was so good. Third, I like to walk through old neighborhoods. That's where you see how people really live. My friends, on the other hand, love shopping, so I tag along and carry the bags. But that's fine. We end up with a good mix, and I come home with a lot of stories.

My first trip abroad was to Osaka, in Japan, with a good friend. It was a long time ago, back in my college days. We were so excited, but I was also nervous about one thing: immigration. I'd heard stories about long lines and tough questions. So I practiced my answers in my head the whole flight. When it was finally my turn, the officer looked at my passport, looked at me, and said in English, "Purpose of visit?" My mind went blank! I said, "Um. eating?" My friend burst out laughing because I sounded so silly. The officer smiled and let us through. After that, the trip was a breeze. We visited the castle, ate a ton of food, and rode the trains. To this day, I still get teased about that moment, but I just blame the jet lag!

My favorite piece of furniture is my old leather armchair. It sits in the corner of my room, right next to my bookshelf. I bought it about ten years ago, and it's seen better days. The leather is cracked, and one of the arms is a little worn. But I could never part with it. It's just so comfortable. When I sink into it, it's like being hugged. I do most of my reading there, with a cup of coffee on a little side table. Sometimes I even fall asleep with a book on my chest! My friends keep asking me to get a new one, but I always say, "No way." To me, it's not just a chair. It's my favorite spot to escape from a busy day.

When I was a kid, we didn't have much furniture. Our house had a big wooden wardrobe, and we ate at a low table sitting on the floor. We called it a "bapsang". At night, we folded it up and laid out blankets on the floor to sleep. With the whole family in one room, it was always packed, so there was no way to have my own desk. I did my homework on the same low table, between dinner and bedtime. Everything we had was sturdy, but it wasn't pretty. Now, it's a completely different story. We have beds, a sofa, a dining table with chairs, and a desk just for me. It's more comfortable, and it looks nicer. But I'll say this: those old pieces had a lot of memories. I wouldn't trade them for anything.

Yes, and it was totally my fault. A couple of years ago, I bought a brand-new white sofa. I loved it, and I gave myself one rule: "No coffee on the sofa!" I followed that rule for about two weeks. Then one morning, I sat down with a big mug of coffee, and I had my laptop on my knees. I got a work call, and I jumped up. Before I knew it, the whole mug tipped over. A big brown stain spread across the cushion. My heart dropped. I panicked, and I started scrubbing with a wet towel, which made it worse. Then I searched online and found a trick with baking soda and vinegar. It helped a lot, but a faint mark was still there. In the end, I bought a nice gray cover, and the stain was gone for good. I felt pretty silly, though. Now I drink my coffee at the table.

I have a favorite cafe near my apartment, and it's a small roastery by the sea. What makes it special is the owner. He roasts his own beans right in the shop, so the whole place smells like heaven. The first time I went there, he asked me, "What kind of coffee do you like?" I said, "Strong and not too sour." He thought for a second, and then he made me a special cup. It was perfect! Now he remembers my order, so I just walk in and he says, "The usual?" It's also right on the water, with big windows. You can watch fishing boats come and go. For a coffee lover, it's paradise. I go there about once a week.

The last time I went to a coffee shop was last Saturday. I went with my friend's kid. He had a test coming up, and he wanted to study outside the house. So we went to a cafe near the library. I ordered an americano, and he got an iced chocolate, because he doesn't like coffee yet. I told him, "Give it a few years!" He opened his books and started studying. I took out a novel I'd been reading. We didn't talk much, but I liked sitting there next to him. After an hour, I bought him a slice of cheesecake, as a reward. He said, "Thanks a lot!" It's moments like that I really treasure.

Let me think. Oh, there's one I'll never forget. One Sunday morning, I walked to a cafe near my apartment. I was in my sweatpants, half asleep, and I just needed my coffee. I ordered a large latte and a croissant. Then, when I reached into my pocket, my wallet wasn't there. I'd left it at home! I tried to pay with my phone, but the battery was at 1 percent, and it died right there. I wanted to disappear. The barista looked at me, and he must have seen how desperate I was. He smiled and said, "Don't worry about it. Pay me next time." I couldn't believe it. I thanked him about five times. The next day, I went back, paid for it, and brought him a bag of good coffee beans as a thank-you. We've been friendly ever since. I learned that small kindness can make your day.

Hi, I'm thinking about joining your gym, and I have a few questions. First, what are your opening hours? I work late, so I need to know if you're open in the evening.. Okay, good. What kind of equipment do you have? I'd like to use treadmills and some weights.. Great. And do you offer any classes, like yoga or spinning?. How much is the monthly membership? Is there a discount for a longer term?. One last thing: do you have showers and lockers?. That sounds perfect. Can I come by for a free trial? Thanks a lot!

Hello, I joined your gym yesterday, and I'm calling because I have some concerns. When I visited, it wasn't what I expected. First, it was really crowded. I had to wait 20 minutes to use a treadmill. Second, two of the machines were out of order, and nobody seemed to care. And third, the locker room was a mess. The showers weren't clean. I understand every gym has its off days, but this isn't what the website showed. I paid for a membership, thinking it'd be a nice, quiet place. So I'd like to ask for a full refund. I haven't used it much, just one visit. Could you please take care of that for me? I'd really appreciate it. Thank you for understanding.

Well, a few years ago, I had my yearly health checkup at work. The doctor looked at my results and said, "Your weight and your blood sugar are a little high." I felt like I'd been slapped! I'd gained about six kilos in a couple of years, mostly from late-night ramyun while I played games. So I decided to go on a diet. At first, I tried skipping dinner. That was a disaster. I got so hungry that I ended up eating a whole bag of chips at midnight. Then I changed my plan. I cut down on late-night snacks, ate smaller portions, and went for a walk after dinner. It was slow, but it worked. After four months, I lost six kilos. The doctor was impressed at my next checkup. I still drink coffee, of course. I'm not a monster!

Five years ago, people mostly used phones for the basics. They sent messages with KakaoTalk, took photos, watched YouTube, and played mobile games. Mobile banking and maps were already popular. But phones were more of a tool. These days, a phone is almost like a second brain. The biggest change is AI. You can talk to an assistant, ask it to write an email, or translate a menu with the camera. I use it at work every day. Another big change is payments. I haven't carried cash for a long time. I just scan a QR code or tap my phone. And short videos have taken over everybody's free time. It's kind of amazing how fast things have changed. Honestly, I'd be lost without my phone.

I think most people in Korea are worried about it. You see it everywhere: at a restaurant, a whole group of teenagers sitting together, and everyone's looking down at their phone. People say young people can't hold a real conversation anymore. Some parents worry about their kids' eyesight, and about being addicted to short videos. I see it at my friends' houses too. At their dinner tables, it's the same story. Everybody has a phone in hand. But I also see the other side. Young people use their phones to make friends, learn new things, and stay in touch. It's their way of socializing. So, when friends come over, we have a simple rule: no phones at the dinner table. It was tough at first, but now we actually talk. I think balance is the key.
